title: Ivo and the Cellar
premise: Marguerite Halloran has spent twelve years in the village of Coldharbour Row, keeping their head down and their surveying work impeccable, while the cellar beneath the old Halloran house makes sounds no house should make. When the church bell—melted down in 1911—rings at midnight, Marguerite learns the founders built the village as a ritual engine, and the Hallorans were meant to be its keepers, feeding it belonging in exchange for protection. The village's warm, suffocating community is revealed as a harvest: every act of inclusion deepens the founders' claim on the residents' souls. To end it, Marguerite must complete the interrupted rite in the cellar, but doing so requires accepting the family name, the family power, and the corruption that comes with both. In the end, Marguerite rings the bell themselves and unbinds the village, choosing exile and grief over the belonging that was always a trap—yet the final pages hint the cellar has simply begun listening elsewhere.
about_author: Sebastian Reyes is a former architectural conservator who spent a decade documenting buildings slated for demolition, a job that taught him houses remember more than people do. He writes horror about the violence of being welcomed, and lives somewhere he refuses to name precisely.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A routine survey of the derelict Halloran house reveals a cellar with fresh footprints in century-old dust. Marguerite documents everything, explains nothing, and declines the vicar's invitation to Sunday supper. Emotional beat: the practiced comfort of professional detachment beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with flashbacks to their arrival in Coldharbour Row after a family estrangement. Each past noise in their own cottage gets a tidy rationalization catalogued like a survey report. Emotional beat: the exhausting labor of not belonging on purpose.

chapters.title: A Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. At midnight the church bell rings; parish records confirm it was melted in 1911. The whole village wakes, and instead of fear, there is joy—neighbors weeping with delight in the street. Emotional beat: Marguerite's isolation becomes visible and dangerous.

chapters.title: Everyone Knows Your Name
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The village turns warmly toward them: gifts on the doorstep, invitations, a reserved pew. Mrs. Aldery, the oldest resident, watches Marguerite with something like hunger. Emotional beat: the horror of being suddenly, perfectly included.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Marguerite and local historian Dev Okonkwo's POV alternates. In the archive they find the founders' ledger: names entered in a rotating order, each marked 'received.' The last Halloran entry is 1911, marked 'interrupted.' Emotional beat: curiosity curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Says
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. They enter the cellar and find a bell-shaped hollow in the stone, warm to the touch, humming with the bell's note. Their name is already scratched faintly into the wall. Emotional beat: the past reaching forward and claiming them by blood.

chapters.title: The Warmth of the Row
chapters.summary: Village ensemble POV. A harvest feast where Marguerite is seated at the center, toasted, loved. Dev, half-drunk, whispers that he checked the ledger twice: everyone marked 'received' died exactly twelve years after their entry. Emotional beat: belonging revealed as a countdown.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldery's Confession
chapters.summary: Mrs. Aldery's POV. She entered the ledger in 1911 as a child—the interruption's witness—and has been 'kept' ever since, neither living nor owed. She tells Marguerite the founders fed the village to the bell and the bell fed them back. Emotional beat: pity for the monster who was also a victim.

chapters.title: The Ritual, Half-Done
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Dev's POV. Reconstructed from the ledger: the rite requires a Halloran to ring the bell and speak the founders' covenant, binding the village's belonging into the bell forever. In 1911, Marguerite's great-grandmother refused mid-rite. Emotional beat: inheritance as indictment.

chapters.title: Doors That Won't Open
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Attempting to leave the village, Marguerite finds every road curving back to Coldharbour Row; the church bell rings each time they cross the boundary stone. Emotional beat: claustrophobic realization that refusal has consequences.

chapters.title: The Vicar's Sermon
chapters.summary: Vicar Ellen Marsh's POV. She knows exactly what the village is; she was 'received' thirty years ago and has kept the congregation complicit ever since, believing the harvest is a fair price for peace. She offers Marguerite the choice, kindly. Emotional beat: power's corruption wearing a compassionate face.

chapters.title: Twelve Years, Marked
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite realizes their arrival twelve years ago was itself an entry in the ledger—the noises, the isolation, all of it the bell 'tendering' them. Dev finds his own name newly inked. Emotional beat: the trap was always already sprung.

chapters.title: What Dev Chose
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Frightened and flattered, Dev attends a 'receiving' for old Tom Wicker and watches the village absorb him—Tom's face going serene, then vacant, then glad. Dev comes to Marguerite ready to burn the ledger. Emotional beat: friendship forged in shared horror.

chapters.title: Burning the Ledger
chapters.summary: Marguerite and Dev's POV. They burn the ledger in the churchyard; the ashes rise in the shape of a bell, and every villager turns as one to look at them, smiling. The bell rings without being struck. Emotional beat: defiance met with terrible patience.

chapters.title: The Village That Loves You
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The village closes around Marguerite and Dev—doors opening, arms opening, everyone speaking in the bell's resonance. Mrs. Aldery dies at last, freed, whispering that only a Halloran can unmake what a Halloran made. Emotional beat: love as siege.

chapters.title: Dev Is Received
chapters.summary: Dev's POV, final entry. Dev chooses to be received in Marguerite's place, buying time, his last lucid words telling Marguerite to finish the rite backwards—ring the bell and refuse the covenant aloud. Emotional beat: sacrifice, and the guilt of accepting it.

chapters.title: The Cellar Remembers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In the cellar, the founders' voices press in—generations of Hallorans who completed the rite elsewhere and grew fat on harvested belonging. They offer Marguerite everything: family, home, Dev restored. Emotional beat: the seduction at the heart of power.

chapters.title: The Covenant Spoken
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite begins the rite as instructed, speaking the founders' words, feeling the village's love pour into them like heat—then stops, one syllable short, as their great-grandmother did in 1911. Emotional beat: the moment of refusal as the true inheritance.

chapters.title: Ring It Backwards
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Climax. Marguerite seizes the bell rope that rises through the cellar floor and rings the unstruck bell, speaking refusal into each peal. The village screams its love as the founders are pulled into the hollow; the vicar ages to dust smiling. Emotional beat: terrible, costly triumph.

chapters.title: Aftermath: Coldharbour Row
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The village wakes ordinary and diminished, grieving people they can't name. Dev is gone; only his handwriting in the ledger's margin remains. The house appraises at nothing. Emotional beat: hollow relief and the price of freedom.

chapters.title: The Surveyor's Report
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Marguerite files a final, truthful survey—cellar: hollow, unexplained—and signs the Halloran name for the first and last time, then leaves on an open road that stays open. Emotional beat: exile chosen over corrupted belonging, grief carried willingly.

chapters.title: A House That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Distant third-person POV. Months later, a surveyor in another county notes warm footprints in a cellar's dust and a hum she can't source. Somewhere, a bell that was never cast rings once. Emotional beat: the quiet horror that hunger for belonging never dies—it relocates.
